content: Consumer credit may be approaching its foundational AI moment — with buy now, pay later emerging as the first visible act. title: Zambia Abandons Plan to Extend IMF Credit Facility by a Year

title: Seed Funding In 2025 Broke Records Around Big Rounds And AI, With US Far In The Lead

Subject: 08/01/26: Solaris verbrennt weitere 100 Mio. , Coba holt Fintech-Promi

Außerdem: Die 2026-Agenda für Fintech, Payment und Digital Banking
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png]
Ausblick (#3): "Der digitale Euro wird kommen  die Banken können sich dem nicht entziehen"
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/08896b25-c6b3-2b3c-37b5-f92ec49d7919.jpg]

Im dritten Teil unserer Jahresausblicks-Serie beleuchten Christian Kirchner und Jochen Siegert alles, was mit digitalem Banking, Fintech und Payment zu tun hat.

#1: Von "Verification of Payee" bis "KI-Compliance"  Jochen Siegert korrigiert den Fintech-Ausblick von ChatGPT

#2: Warum klassische VC-Investoren die Lust an German Fintech so ein bisschen verloren haben

#3: Trade Republic und Revolut sind die großen Gewinner der letzten Jahre  welche To-dos warten 2026 auf sie?

#4: Welche Fintechs von der KI angegriffen werden  und wie sie sich wehren können (Servicing!)

#5: Auch wenn die KI bisweilen halluziniert  im Kunden-Support gibt's für die Banken keinen Weg zurück

#6: Paypal, Klarna oder gar die Volksbanken  wer macht Apple Pay die Kunden-Schnittstelle streitig?

#7: Wero wird auch in diesem Jahr noch viel Grundlagenarbeit leisten müssen. Geht das Zeitfenster bereits zu?

#8: Wie lange werden sich unsere Banken noch gegen den digitalen Euro wehren? (These: Womöglich gar nicht mehr so lange)

Das Jahr begann für Anlegerinnen und Anleger gleich mit einem Superlativ: Erstmals stieg der deutsche Leitindex Dax am gestrigen Mittwoch über die Marke von 25.000 Punkten. Die KI-Euphorie an der Börse ist offenbar ungebrochen, hinzu kommen Investments in den Rüstungssektor, die insbesondere nach dem Überfall der USA auf Venezuela in den vergangenen Tagen noch einmal zugenommen haben.

Mein Kollege Christoph Rottwilm hat den aktuellen Höhenflug zum Anlass genommen, sich die Entwicklung des Dax der vergangenen Monate genau anzuschauen. In welche Aktien stecken Privatanleger am meisten Geld? Welche Strategie brachte dabei den größten Erfolg und was können Anleger aus dem Dax-Rekord lernen? Die Analyse meines Kollegen lesen Sie hier: Umsätze, Kurse, Timing  der Weg des Dax zum Höchststand (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e86338360c8b0fda4638108e400438b4e9408c9a1aa6e872f0f62e26ef7ae058f06542d5336af3c4c0146183a41d98ee14445d6f268393b5f87432d4>.

Die Wirtschaftsnews des Tages:

  *   Angesichts sehr sorgenvoller und gefährlicher Zeiten würde US-Präsident Donald Trump (79) für das Haushaltsjahr 2027 gern das Militärbudget erhöhen <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e86338367d2410c470e391fb0b15ebe2141c5c8faced1ca63db5c311f3c9db1c00aac1ffcb82c63ccca4350294b67cc3784959c18885da18a0fd1318> (von derzeit ungefähr einer Billion US-Dollar auf 1,5 Billionen). Zudem kritisierte er eine aus seiner Sicht schleppende Produktion der US-Rüstungsunternehmen. Trump will mehr Druck auf die Industrie ausüben und bis auf Weiteres Dividendenausschüttungen sowie Aktienrückkäufe verbieten. Zunächst blieb allerdings unklar, wie der US-Präsident diese Verbote durchsetzen möchte.

  *   Chinesische Unternehmen sollen mehr als zwei Millionen Stück des beliebten KI-Chips H200 von Nividia bestellt haben. Der US-Hersteller liefert die Halbleiter laut einem Agenturbericht aber nur noch bei Vorauszahlung nach China<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e86338362fe2d076118b632f11eace03ca4c9907311ab9ec61c3f950cc52719d1d801d7e9c92d0b213532f378ac6211c660a438ccd23d943304d3fb9>. Damit wolle sich das Unternehmen gegen Unsicherheiten bei der Genehmigung von Lieferungen durch die chinesischen Behörden absichern.

  *   Zalando schließt Ende September sein Logistikzentrum in Erfurt mit 2700 Beschäftigten <https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e8633836b9d609e3385270586acca5122ddbe0ca8ccb5feb583e87e168a35738f3bb7f8bcf65ae1ffbd3d21d3a481963f00c7f302b6469ccb54c58a4> . Der Modeversandhändler richtet sein Logistiknetzwerk neu aus. Was das für die betroffenen Beschäftigten bedeutet, ist aktuell unklar.

  *   Start-up-Gründungen in Deutschland sind 2025 auf einen Rekordwert gestiegen<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e86338360ba82721603a31c5ca4ed6371f19b0d55eaf01a160be9a463d91fd704d3f22161ea97b51f8f00a96425cd6bdb06d2b624e97e1c8f9a9bc65>. Die Zahlen liegen demnach noch höher als im Boomjahr 2021, als die Coronapandemie für einen Digitalisierungsschub sorgte. Grund für die neuen Rekordzahlen ist die Euphorie um künstliche Intelligenz.

[separator]
Die Personalien des Tages:

  *   Als Strategiechefin bei Audi legte Silja Pieh (51) unter dem damaligen CEO Markus Duesmann (56) ab 2020 die Grundlagen zum Ausstieg der Marke aus der Verbrennertechnologie. Das Duo hatte sich vorgenommen, bereits ab 2033 keine Neuwagen mit Benzin- oder Dieselmotoren zu verkaufen. Mittlerweile arbeiten beide nicht mehr für den Automobilkonzern. Stattdessen will Pieh nun als Klimalobbyistin die Transformation vorantreiben, wie mein Kollege Christoph Neßhöver erfahren hat (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e8633836a02cdb8f4a294d44c5bd8e1097c01fd8776f161f393ef44ce51acef9a8b56f591f5b5a228aede01ae5481a4ff319f2ff14404a6110df6c85>.

  *   Olaf Koch (55) trieb seit einem knappen Jahr als Verwaltungsratsvorsitzender den Generationenwechsel beim Medienkonzern Hubert Burda Media voran. Nun trennen sich Elisabeth Burda Furtwängler (33) und Jacob Burda (35) allerdings von ihm und berufen Marc Al-Hames (47) an die Spitze. Auch den Vorstand krempeln sie um<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=82dbdc89e863383688cb84b19fc1297befdf2021008c97493a204aa8ca252c159eb69a478a498a4cd5de972ff837bc099799b960541c734e55f1eec26c902859>, wie meine Kollegen Henning Hinze und Theodor Harzer erfahren haben.

MoviePass Economy II

Back in the 2010s, we used<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/P3-Z_iWROYLNZy22CZc_BFipk-bwl6bncCOojpZu6kKapA-tVa9hFC2UBWGSZSjx1UCW7rC8RBGT3DJ-kGBQRwsiHyoMiXs0QsLmfnni0cTL37wvHUFLf-2IxdhYaspZiE1TXBwisevoXlt0MfDA8Y2sg0bov0sMzWAZLDDqxQdbNsndndfxu15uqJifoMNX82HkDX2KqhmBwII79B8ZTo_qYB8H_KugE4NjT-tOaAUMXol1M6oAbhn8LDtM5PmOZFCIC5u-wfZFO8ZkPPK7X7_-EOJefg8L7Hotkdw_JpJT17mirBquWeORMXuSqzLFIbFsc6JWsDfqeYxtDMte8kmUCZYtdQ1xrdkhiD0l4LZeP1yHk_gjZHBRyQ/SwUuLMYhESGqF_tREgeZUnxTAyCuoAXP/16> to<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/ybrYYxf0ng7109svvCnE_5gFa8N2OAucE2miPg7cOKH435bMol4T2oeZEkeyREmIfF3FmI8nGEFz5yZa_VXtE4i4gGkgkLCRbAFUeaTeiqQtSqZpH1Uf-99e93qssN5Hx-oSw4ajSzjfqO_jrgCijWo35UQhwQRSxSQlVYeucIYrQ3U1G4H5Y0JoGFfZyzqGohCyEwf8Pl56sAbEv0HptGcSbcG30csejdbalLyszAMMk9zc9V20QdhOxvwwqSEoD0sr-5g_ysTFlEmruY4aOg7JzFSqpi6pqNFtWA5klghv57FaoT-2sNvO5peY9RUhTB-IzWn89cdIszCm3qRASnDhT84arsIMtpTJ7CI9bpPZAq5CwFYN_JgcxQ/jZHevQblP6Z4v6Dps7IxhJB-NaWRt2Yq/16> talk<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/G-S1fABBm0QGLRj5j5hslg6TpogW8It3uCeCd4Pc6uCsE4b3pyqnpmdXylGaZg2pLQ65W5YSfO-ZR1JFBNOpBGEoogHMwq3sW_dWjOiL82P2qDVwqD89f80JQlaTqCwoOGsjSHZ7GsbbNN2Sg4TDBGnm9pmQUA0zyOPnhv-lXC3YhG6TVeYSuDKaAsI067DVoSCEXlupzQboqrYLgIOLZvckK05oB1PEVWiJS6Q2KoLMaTaUcFwphVXg0zZ2S1Jg5AO5xA4yGJTYfh-V4zm00i0hiibujfre1ddSU8kvut9s3rDtcJE0SMNscJ1f1QmUmKj0TOWxASR8NOFuQp-wqlZfzEgI9CMmRZiQA5PfOUvJdlSVIVM-a0Ktow/9Fa09ty9ATIjJIBbZE9XQQ9-AQYf-VLd/16> about<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/foRQhpuYOFsmk-mzySynXEYppTRndlGvre8hK01294-_5KA5sO9MWb2_GTrFYad3eR_14WmJMRXPptjb-w7qRwhuv9HiCCJMn-mS1ad_Bm43uXTLLQSOM3z_hTeGGNrrdNhEMsL96j5BbRKGJK2iRlfy0KP3FML4z6DCeHHW_OfGry31dX3m1oQiOrz-M-AL8ZQ7qB0Ag10D9dGi0UCQfUS-5nne84Oly3P_wbPGJv_enJ4kDd5_x9Md1eV4Nj7WBEJyFsCBwpRoFVTqT0bjFSLpRlbOtzVD1FqQ9UWF5-HDR5u1LqL12x8I2oI1FFEoAlemkCr6i-crEv42FQPVl-szL4PG0pqyIvrzCaSoqpCB-8Vb1ceyoKgKkw/6ugnqLRIKU6IAJ9H92Mu4xYI5pNwN2Zn/16> the MoviePass economy. There was a company called MoviePass. Its core business model was that you paid it $9.95 per month, and in exchange you got to see as many movies as you wanted in theaters. Movie tickets, back then, usually cost $12 or so, so if you saw even one movie a month this was a good deal for you. How was MoviePass able to offer you that deal? Uh. It went and paid full price for the movie tickets and lost money on every customer<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/nX4q1AoJ_yn7mb5k-FnNVfiRApo01qX_5OpCEeVey00qzXy0eEpQM9Q1l6hypaNUpapafBb2wThE9NV9WwMSkXrj3vamWScehIh6WUmPa8x7YKB00OqpzEykZQEzvN5sJOdL1lIG52N6wMZgobKIUeyjlu3PfpDdCZCm892KYT-AdJXAXvq9cvnrZcq8Edg_MRcUbo7B2RTUQ0UyxdS_0_jxFDd-TIPvIYzEu0hpo2_6NNcu6mJTPIQw2pToBmSXXGKwfwV8fWOmTEGOgBa97pOEoTkWCh34MdRoOy8A_A0xX38GQ0XlF2ZATnq063HMvDIghlty1T11OK9HRJxdA6uC-oCf4mB10cMqowNs3PTBCmwJdz87Vmqyig/BA3zFKCzdXcX2D9dOEztFunYWWnw3dZq/16>. How was that sustainable? Uh! Some of the answers to that question are:

  1.  Lol it obviously wasnt.
  2.  Big data, MoviePass would occasionally say, with the opposite of a straight face<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/jlRatzFP-LUyNvAcHJAr3U-u6CXs6CMw4YSiY8NPC3wlEuGx_Vafbcufn2OLOa5oPBWmo0P3xC1opXEG4J_ccDVju-xEIgdn4j3IujK7dtW2E6QY4d-SXI4fWFPrjXyMhKDmo8G3sx_e0WPMFJ8f_4qVxUgPDvKEegKtKc6DCMesAT8c5f3hX4g7L-NFcPgNRe7zJL6qSLylZloujdPwRyizOY6Wzq1zN7GPg8dv0Kk9GKLOKe3gXR2f88GdcfPGamT3GD_El185eGVegbD_9ER4bN7dVWiefaOevCOHb4UY4orUrKpPQeCPL2BRZnhU8WpvsFM6ZwrZrJBO7OBwqR2WAJtRykCUClx3OCguiDpCdtfwwFxo2yQHY7I/E_tI5FjPq68RY4yMnuHk79p4znUChaW-/16>: When you signed up for its service, MoviePass obtained some data about you, which it could  something  something  something. MoviePass itself never bothered to complete that sentence, but in the 2010s data is the new oil was a thing that people (including MoviePass) sometimes said, so maybe this pitch was compelling.
  3.  For a while, MoviePass would improve its unit economics by secretly changing peoples passwords to lock them out of their accounts. That way, (1) they couldnt buy any movie tickets, (2) they were still paying $9.95 per month and (3) they couldnt cancel. This really happened<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/ZloROlZIPBSllhS1HItfb0MCyvOxCoIIJgC2CvGnH_mgb6V7_77VtqTu6KX8y5ZMBePtIp4gdBo9h-knkmVOaP2IKDiM492KUlfCG55BhvxodPN7-fTZN0MDW07IQFoj5Z_jmST_B8NpBVPLrw961hktmtL2Jx3tYcSyhUyl6pDd7gtFmnGeoao7589Xu03Nh4r-VLRMrkfTstxIGlsAwJJk9cPWI7FQGDoeT-q3YSbtFV1EbweK9DSfjQKBaePEe-l-0uSQoEBF1WXH8ZLnLn3yr-yS4ydwI0TlLef_a9SldY_dxb3_o5nHl_DplfiMI6WDUbU2YEMnSmfgBdjnu0aqz80gbZ2iB5Cgr1uiN5RU5OJoMY1o64Uq7oc/R4zbpi50_n-0veppmgUTcTovvJad9foA/16>!
  4.  At a higher level of generality, MoviePasss business model was sustainable, for a while, because its investors were willing to sustain it. MoviePass could lose money on every customer every month, because investors thought there was a plausible business model in there somewhere. Eventually, they thought, something something something. Eventually MoviePass would strike deals with theaters to lower its costs. Eventually it would find some ancillary revenues. Eventually the data would pay off. Something! The point, in the 2010s, was rapid user growth. There are no second acts in American lives. Just dont tell MoviePass co-founder and CEO Stacy Spikes. 

In 2021, Spikesin a redemption arc he likens to Steve Jobs at Apple and Michael Dell at Dellbought back the assets of his company out of bankruptcy, once valued at around $500 million, for $140,000. 

Users can now subscribe to multiple plans, including a $33-a-month tier that allows up to four movies. ...

A former Miramax VP of marketing, Spikes tells me he realized MoviePasss future couldnt be built on just movie tickets. ...

If MoviePass couldnt match the big chains, then what? The answer, as Ive seen before, came from the predictions market, or as Spikes says, through gamification.

The speculation market is projected to become a trillion-dollar ecosystem by the end of the decade. If MoviePass could claim even a sliver of that attention, Spikes reasoned, it could offset long-term decline in its core subscription businessa crucial hedge as the theatrical industry continues to struggle.

Hes got a movie prediction market thingy called Mogul:

Mogul is not intended to be a competitor to the Kalshis and Polymarkets of the world, which Spikes likens to the NASDAQ and New York Stock Exchange. He wants to be the specific category or volume play that feeds into those larger exchanges, rather than carrying the massive capital and licensing burden required to be a complete marketplace. The goal is also for Mogul to funnel into MoviePass and boost the subscription service. Over 630,000 users were on the waitlist to join the Mogul platform, while roughly 5,000 users played the initial private beta version that launched last May. The plan for Mogul to make money is initially through contest fees for fantasy sports-style competitions, subscription tiers that unlock reduced contest fees and access to limited-entry contests and tokenized trading transactions. Eventually, Spikes hopes studios will sponsor or partner on contests tied to film releases.

There is an important difference between these two sources of capital, the public SPAC investors and the PIPE investors. The SPAC investors gave M3-Brigade their money in July 2024, and they can get it back: They bought shares at $10 per share, the $10 is sitting in a trust and earning interest, and, when the ReserveOne merger closes, the SPAC investors can choose either to keep their shares (which become shares of ReserveOne) or to get back their $10, with interest. (The merger has not closed yet, but the redemption would have been worth $10.61<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/_L-ecDfX_qTjtfU7XybLnoe5r1d75Wj56cT2V2wjZyi1ZAgVpfI0blcDs-xTUPVctpiG1pCn1_2Rdbi62i2bkNlnEPuAaGW73Au9hFtbFPgVj_ef3JW7jZhoaqbvaQuWXTp8Md6Hy7zICY4hJEeNOra1lQ_Uc3WS39S3Fg2LxpjLAtcjGf1IIE7fpmWMyRGOEMQ56kPufDUgDW5ypMqbS2GgaAfzWqTUetmeh8LLJ6POdVkHOYyYGRg3xDDuiflQ0hbRjmNEErKap317GlVKiEZOsGEJaA-RtHf2vojNkD68XekufPY-ZkiMXN4ISkT-tF8LCgqnaynkVa-RqXKQA8zQvsvhRW1dBS78PixlLBDNlG_1mP2QMRwnIfg/3AU95Snm6XzAyhHVxO2F4ws3hvQ8SNGS/16> as of the end of October, and it keeps earning interest so its worth more now.) The SPAC investors were giving M3-Brigade a blank check, but not quite: They handed M3-Brigade $287.5 million to buy whatever company it wanted, but they  like all SPAC investors  reserved the right to take their money back if they didnt like the deal.

Also, the SPAC investors get to vote on the deal: M3-Brigades management signed a merger agreement with ReserveOnes management, but M3-Brigades public shareholders get to vote on the deal before it closes. The vote is in a sense independent of the redemption right: SPAC shareholders can vote for the deal and redeem their shares. This creates somewhat weird incentives. If all of the SPAC shareholders hate the deal, they might vote against it, and then it wont close. But it might be more rational for them all to vote for the deal, so that it does close, and then redeem their shares for $10.61. [2] (Historically, SPAC mergers often contained minimum cash provisions, saying that if more than X% of the SPAC shareholders redeemed, the deal was off, but as SPAC investors have gotten flightier those have gone away.)

The PIPE investors, on the other hand, havent given M3-Brigade any money yet: They have signed agreements to put up their money once the merger closes. And they did not give M3-Brigade a blank check: They invested specifically in this deal, they had the chance to do due diligence, and they knew exactly what they were signing up for. And so they dont have redemption rights, or a vote: They already signed on for the ReserveOne deal, so theres no need for them to vote on it, and no reason to let them out of the deal. They are fully committed. If the merger closes, they have to close on their funding.

Anyway, like I said, everyone signed up for this in July 2025, when lets put some crypto in a pot and sell shares was a normal and lucrative thing to think. But the deal hasnt closed yet, and that is no longer an especially lucrative thing to think. If you put $1 billion of crypto into a pot, the shares of that pot will be worth, like, $950 million. If you put $10 in this deal, you might have an immediate loss. (Not investing advice!)

And its worse than that. The actual math is more like this:

Those cuts  more than $100 million for Chu and Cantor  dilute the value that the other shareholders get. The other shareholders probably means the PIPE investors, since the SPAC shareholders can just redeem and get their cash back. The PIPE investors will put in $750 million to get, you know, 85% of a pot of $750 million worth of crypto (which might be worth $700 million on the stock market). Not a great trade, or not anymore.

In July, the PIPE investors agreed to pay $10 per share of a DAT that they figured would trade at $15 or $20. But the DAT market collapsed, and that looks less attainable now.

But the merger hasnt closed yet! They havent bought the crypto! Everyone could just walk away. Never mind, putting $750 million into a pot to buy crypto is not the great trade we thought it was, forget it. Presumably the PIPE investors would like that. The problem is that M3-Brigades sponsor wants the deal to close (it gets like $70 million worth of stock if it does), and Cantor Fitzgerald wants the deal to close (it gets like $30 million of fees if it does), even if the deal is not actually good for the regular investors. Meanwhile the SPAC shareholders dont care one way or the other: Whether or not the deal closes, they can get their $10 back with interest.

But the SPAC shareholders, who dont care, get a vote on whether the deal closes. The PIPE shareholders dont. (The sponsor does: Its 7.2 million founder shares get to vote on the deal, and in fact it has signed a support agreement<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/NlZ-gsVQmKtL12BHXnw5ESsR1Kkbge1TVhT6Jie27EDq_39WZqaRlZB--tXq9bz4HjZ8E3Z7v0cB2QZgfIB0aJCCt6ftPLUudgJUKQ9kg0wxq_5ZZuidUKCdVyJsj30G52sFXrLvhA_FoDGu9HSpaCxnR28pIwL9BOAzhXYWUz74XIZaWyC8e0wsWQjUSQ_GBkgqZd7tU0TkoCWrgut5CebillM_QpnQn-cn7vGn4zUxC0mlHPRUngYDDIR-0vsgX5hmnXbPhmJ_iG8EGI-693XOKkAgKUNRqcrk5E6riDHaeQ3dDLLyDFrh8zMxhowv5tBZQTWhk79VQS8lzXnQC7yX5gSSTuywX-3yzwrmRUJVuQ6-axB9GfecgTE/WdnDp2AIX348Qh23sIfAypOJlvYVGCAN/16> promising to vote for it, meaning that 20% of the vote is effectively locked up in favor of the deal.) Which means that, if you are a PIPE investor who no longer likes the deal, there might be a way out:

  *   Buy shares of M3-Brigade in the open market. They have traded between $10.63 and $10.89, give or take, over the last month.

Instead of betting the Bills will beat the Jaguars, you bet the Bills will beat the Jaguars and Josh Allen will throw for at least two touchdowns and the total score will be at least 68 points and , etc. The sportsbook will give you a menu of things that might happen in the game, and youll pick like 10 of them and bet $20, and if they all happen youll win like $10,000, but if even one of them doesnt happen you lose your $20. People seem to love these bets, and mostly lose, so they are very lucrative for the sportsbooks.

These are fundamentally correlation trades: The price of a bet like the Bills will beat the Jaguars depends on the probability of that happening, but the price of a bet like the Bills will beat the Jaguars and Josh Allen will throw two touchdowns depends on the probability of each of those things happening and their correlation. DraftKings told regulators that a patron had strung together a series of "Total Hit" wagers on Toronto Blue Jays player Nathan Lukes during the 2025 American League Championship Series. The patron used them to form several multi-leg parlays. His bets hit when the player finished with nine hits in the 7-game series against Seattle.

A review of the wagering data showed 27 parlays tied to the error. Of those, 24 would have resulted in full payouts totaling roughly $828,104.77 if all correlated legs were honored. Only three parlays included losing, non-correlated legs  tied to college football outcomes involving Clemson, Florida State, and Miami.

The book told regulators that a trader mistakenly allowed those "total hit" wagers to be strung together in multi-leg parlays. The "total hit" parlays of 5, 6, 7 and 8 hits in the series were combined with high-probability NFL money line wagers to boost their payout.

What was the probability that Nathan Lukes would get at least six hits in the ALCS? I dont know, some number, lets say 50%. What was the probability that he would get at least seven hits? Some lower number; thats harder to do. What was the probability that, if he got at least seven hits, he would get at least six hits? Obviously 100%. DraftKings seems to have priced the he gets five hits and six hits and seven hits and eight hits bet at much longer odds than the simple he gets eight hits bet, which is a rookie mistake.

To be fair, this seems to have been an error not in its correlation models but in, uh, something else:

The issue stemmed from a misclassification that labeled Lukes as a non-participant rather than an active player in the sportsbooks Player to Record X+ Hits in Series markets. That designation allowed a single trader to bypass built-in safeguards designed to prevent bettors from parlaying correlated outcomes from the same market.

As a result, bettors were able to combine multiple Lukes hit-threshold props into one wager  including 5+ hits (-303), 6+ hits (-105), 7+ hits (+235), and 8+ hits (+550). Functionally, the parlays created a single, inflated wager on Lukes recording eight or more hits in the series, but at dramatically enhanced odds.

If the sportsbook messes that up, can it take back the bet? DraftKings tried to void these bets, and some state gaming regulators let it, but others did not.
